texts.title: The return of the night train

paragraphs.text: For most of the twentieth century the sleeper was an ordinary way to cross Europe. You boarded in one capital in the evening, ate in the dining car, and woke up in another. Then, in the 1990s, cheap flights arrived, and the night train began to look like a museum piece. One operator after another withdrew its sleeping cars: between 2000 and 2015 dozens of routes were cut, and several national railways left the business altogether. The rolling stock was sold, scrapped or left to rust in sidings. What happened next surprised almost everyone. From about 2016 the direction of travel reversed. An Austrian operator bought sleeping cars that a larger neighbour no longer wanted, put them back on the rails, and began adding routes rather than closing them.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: To understand why the sleeper nearly died, it helps to look at the arithmetic rather than the romance. A carriage full of seats can hold eighty passengers; the same carriage fitted with berths holds perhaps thirty, and a carriage of single compartments holds fewer still. Staff must be on board through the night, which no daytime service requires. The train needs a path across the network at the very hours when engineers want the track to themselves, because maintenance of the track is usually carried out at night. And the vehicles themselves are specialised: a sleeping car cannot be used for anything else, so it earns money only when the route runs.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The return of the sleeper has less to do with nostalgia than with carbon. A short flight releases far more greenhouse gas per passenger than the equivalent rail journey, and by the end of the 2010s enough travellers had noticed for the shift to show up in ticket sales. In Sweden a word for the unease of flying entered ordinary speech. Large companies began to write rail into their travel policies, partly to cut reported emissions and partly because staff asked for it. Governments moved too: one European country has banned domestic flights on routes where the train takes under two and a half hours. None of these measures was aimed at night trains in particular, but together they changed the question a traveller asks from “how fast?” to “at what cost?”.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Operators who studied their own passengers found that comfort mattered less than they had assumed. What people wanted was sleep and privacy, in that order, and to be delivered somewhere useful. A night train sets its passengers down in the city centre at breakfast time, with no airport transfer at either end, and passengers value arriving in the city centre far more than they value a wider bed. The newest vehicles answer this directly. Alongside the traditional six-berth couchette there are now single compartments for travellers who do not want to share with strangers, sealed pods with a door and a locker, and quieter bogies, because a passenger who is woken four times has not really travelled overnight at all.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The obstacles that remain are mostly administrative. A night train crosses three or four borders while its passengers sleep, and the operator needs approval from the regulator in every country it passes through, under rules that were written for freight and commuter traffic. Electrical systems and signalling still differ from one network to the next, so a locomotive that works in one country may be useless in the next. Then there is the queue for vehicles: the factories that build sleeping cars are few, and an order placed today is delivered in years, not months. Night services must also compete with freight trains for space on the network at night, and freight has the older claim.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: It would be easy to oversell all this. The sleeper is not going to replace aviation, and the routes that work are a particular shape: long enough that the journey fills a night, short enough that it does not fill two. Between roughly 800 and 1,500 kilometres the night train is competitive; beyond that the plane wins on time and below it the day train wins on convenience. The honest measure of the revival is therefore not how many routes are announced, which is easy, but whether a route survives a decade, which is not. On that measure the evidence is encouraging but thin, and the next ten years will settle the argument better than any forecast can.
paragraphs.label: F

texts.title: How honey bees choose a home

paragraphs.text: In late spring a honey bee colony that has outgrown its home divides. About half the workers leave with the old queen and settle on a branch nearby in a cluster the size of a football. The cluster is a temporary thing: it has no comb, no store of honey and no shelter, and if it is still hanging there in a week the bees will die. From this cluster a few hundred of the oldest workers fly out as scouts, and within a day or two the swarm will move, in one flight, to a cavity that none of the other bees has seen. The colony is therefore about to take the most consequential decision of its life, with no leader, no plan and no way of comparing the options side by side.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: What a scout is looking for turns out to be surprisingly precise. She measures the inside of a hollow tree by walking over its surfaces and by making short flights across it in the dark, and she is measuring against a specification. The cavity should hold about forty litres: much smaller and the colony cannot store enough honey for winter, much larger and it cannot keep the space warm. The entrance should be small, a few square centimetres, so that it can be defended, and it should be several metres above the ground, away from most animals that raid nests. The cavity must be dry and it must be sound. A scout that finds all of this in one place has found something rare.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: A scout that is satisfied returns to the cluster and dances on its surface. The dance is the same one bees use for flowers: a figure of eight whose straight run points towards the site and whose length encodes the distance. What matters for the decision is how long the dancer keeps dancing. A site that only just meets the specification earns a handful of circuits; an excellent one earns dozens, repeated over many minutes. The scout is not describing the site in detail. She is advertising it with an effort proportional to how good she judges it to be, and other idle scouts in the cluster read that effort and fly off to look for themselves.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: This is where a crowd of opinions becomes a single choice. A scout that returns from a second visit dances a little less than she did the first time, and less again after the third, so every advertisement fades unless it is renewed. Sites that impress few visitors lose their dancers within hours. Sites that impress many gain them faster than they lose them, and the cluster gradually falls silent about everything except one hollow tree. Crucially, the bees do not wait for agreement. The choice is settled by a quorum: once about fifteen scouts are found at one site at the same time, that site has won, even though most of the swarm has never been there and some scouts are still dancing for somewhere else.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Reaching the quorum changes what the scouts do. They fly back and move through the cluster producing a thin, rising sound that researchers call piping, pressing themselves against their motionless sisters as they go. The piping is not an instruction about direction; it is an instruction about time. A bee cannot fly until the muscles in her thorax are close to thirty-five degrees, and warming them takes several minutes. Piping tells the cluster to warm its flight muscles, and about ten minutes later ten thousand bees lift off together. Only then do the scouts, now flying as guides through the cloud of their sisters, steer the swarm towards the site they chose.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Does the system actually work? The test is blunt: a colony that chooses badly does not survive the winter, and the cost of a poor cavity is paid months after the decision is made. Researchers have measured this by offering swarms a choice of wooden boxes of known size and following the colonies afterwards. Swarms nearly always take the box that matches the specification, even when a poorer box is closer, and colonies in the right-sized boxes are far more likely to be alive in spring. When a swarm is given only poor options it takes one anyway, because hanging on a branch is not an option at all, and those colonies do badly.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The reason this small piece of natural history is quoted so often outside biology is the shape of the procedure rather than the bees. The scouts assess the options independently, each seeing a site for herself before saying anything about it. They advertise in proportion to what they found, so a weak case fades on its own instead of having to be defeated. And the group stops when enough of its members have converged, not when the last doubter has been persuaded. Committees that copy the first two habits and ignore the third tend to talk until someone gives way; the bees are on the wing by then, which is perhaps the most useful thing about them.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: Ask who speaks English and the honest answer is: mostly people who learned it later. By any reasonable count, speakers who acquired English as a second or foreign language outnumber those who grew up with it by something like three to one, and most conversations held in English today take place with no first-language speaker present at all. A meeting between a Korean engineer and a Brazilian buyer is not an unusual case of English use; it is the ordinary case. This simple arithmetic has an awkward consequence for language teaching, which has spent a century treating the speech of a minority as the target that everyone else should aim at. It also raises a question that sounds philosophical and is in fact entirely practical: if English now belongs mostly to the people who learned it, whose version of it should a classroom teach?
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Ana Duarte has spent twenty years arguing that the target is wrong. The purpose of learning English, she says, is to be understood by whoever is in the room, and the room is rarely in London. From recordings of international meetings she has drawn up what she calls a core: the features of pronunciation that actually carry meaning between speakers of different first languages. Get those right, she argues, and your accent is your own business. A national model should not be the target of teaching, because it asks learners to spend years on features that no listener in their working life will need, and it quietly tells them that their own voice is a defect to be corrected.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Martin Keel is not persuaded, and his objection is practical rather than sentimental. Ask learners what they want, he says, and a large majority name a national model, usually British or American; teachers who offer them something else are overruling the people who paid for the course. Worse, the institutions that decide learners’ futures have not moved. Examiners, universities and employers still listen with an ear trained on those models, and a candidate who has been taught an international variety is judged by a standard nobody taught her. Until the gatekeepers change, he argues, teaching to an international core leaves learners short of what they are actually measured against.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Ruth Oyelaran suspects that both of them are arguing about the wrong thing. The dispute looks like a question about pronunciation, she writes, but it is really a question about authority: who writes the textbooks, who sets the tests, whose usage gets printed as an error in the margin. English in Nigeria and India is not a stage on the way to something else. These are varieties with their own settled norms, their own literatures and their own generations of speakers who learned them at home, and describing them as approximations tells you nothing about the language and a good deal about who is doing the describing. The point is not that every variety is equally useful in every room, but that the map of correctness is drawn by somebody, and the somebody is rarely the speakers being corrected.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Tomas Vrba brings evidence rather than argument. In his experiments, listeners from a dozen language backgrounds hear recordings that have been altered one feature at a time, and he measures what they actually fail to understand. The results are uneven in a useful way. Consonants at the beginning of words, and the difference between long and short vowels, cause real breakdowns when they go wrong; vowel quality, the feature that most accent training concentrates on, causes remarkably few. Word stress in long words matters more than either. A teacher with limited hours, he concludes, can now choose what to fix on evidence instead of on habit. None of this settles the argument about ownership, but it does narrow the part of the argument that a timetable has to answer.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Where does this leave a classroom on Monday morning? Not, honestly, in a settled place. The examinations that decide admissions are slow to change and still reward a familiar sound, so Keel’s objection has force whatever one thinks of the principle. But the published descriptions of what has to be taught have narrowed, and the evidence about what actually interrupts understanding is better than it was. Perhaps the most useful thing a teacher can do is stop treating the question as general. A learner who wants to work in a hospital in Manchester and a learner who will spend her career in meetings between Jakarta and Frankfurt do not need the same pronunciation course, and pretending otherwise serves neither of them. The question worth asking in a staffroom is therefore not whose English is correct, but what this particular learner has to be able to do with it.
paragraphs.label: F
